Tooltip_craft_saltingTubDesc: Cures up to 50 weight or 35 pieces of salt-packed fish or meat, never both at once, under a weighted board: 1 to 2 days, longer for bigger pieces; the long country cure of meat takes 10 to 21 days. Nothing more goes in until the cured batch is taken out.
Tooltip_craft_dryingFrameDesc: Hangs up to 8 stacks of fish or meat, up to 2.5 weight each. Salt Cured fish dries in 12 to 30 days, fastest in warm, dry weather. Corned meat dries to charque in summer sun. Gutted fish needs a cold season, or it spoils. Rain stops the drying in the open.
Tooltip_craft_dryingBeamMediumDesc: Hangs up to 4 stacks of fish or meat, up to 15 weight each, on hooks. Dries like a Drying Frame, for pieces too big to hang on one. In the open, under a roof, in a room or in a basement.
Tooltip_craft_dryingBeamLargeDesc: Hangs up to 2 stacks of fish or meat, up to 50 weight each, on hooks. Dries like a Drying Frame, for the biggest pieces. Open air or under an open roof, not in a room.
Tooltip_craft_hangFishToDry: Salt drying, for Salt Cured fish. Works in any season, fastest in warm, dry air, best in the shade. Comes out as Salt Dried fish; in the Smokehouse as Hot Smoked fish with the Firebox stoked, or Cold Smoked with its hours of smoke. Keeps for months.
Tooltip_craft_hangFishToColdDry: Cold drying, for gutted fish and halves. Needs a cold season, out of a room, or the fish rots. Comes out as Stockfish, which keeps for about a year. Not in the Smokehouse.
Tooltip_TraditionalPreservationFishMeat_: Takes 2 salt for each quarter weight of the packed fish, about a seventh of its weight. Carry the salt yourself: a shaker holds 10, a Bag of Salt 50. A fish over 4.5 weight is too thick to salt whole: gut and split it first.
Cure it in a Salting Tub before it spoils.
Cured, but not yet preserved. Rinse off the salt if you like (right-click), then hang it on a drying station or in the Smokehouse.
Hang it to cold dry in a cold season, out of a room, or cook it. Split it if it's too heavy to hang.
Hang it to cold dry in a cold season, out of a room, or cook it.
Keeps for about a year. Too hard to eat: rehydrate it in water first.
Keeps for about a year. Too hard to eat: rehydrate it in water first. Maturing: 0 percent. Matured stockfish cheers you up once rehydrated.
Keeps for about a year. Too hard to eat: rehydrate it in water first. Maturing: 10 percent. Matured stockfish cheers you up once rehydrated.

Keeps for months. Very salty: rehydrate it in water before cooking.
Raw, it will make you sick. Cook it, or add it to a soup or stew. It can't be dried. It also makes chum.

Fish head stock. Its first ingredient makes it a soup or a stew, with up to 6 ingredients and your seasonings. It starts out tastier than a plain soup or stew and takes the boredom off. Cook it before eating.
Tooltip_craft_rinseSaltedFish: Optional. Soaks the excess salt off Salt Cured fish or cured meat (Corned or Country Cured) before hanging, as on the Volga and in the charqueadas. It comes out less salty (less thirst; the fish loses its sharp tang) but keeps a tenth less long. Near a sink, bathtub, barrel or well, right-click it for Rinse at Sink.
Tooltip_TraditionalPreservationFishMeat_: Rinses %1 pieces with %2 L of clean water from the sink, bathtub, barrel or well close by. It comes out less salty but keeps a tenth less long.
Tooltip_craft_stockfishPalletDesc: Where stockfish ripens, stacked as in the old warehouses. Cold Dried fish on it ripens twice as fast in a loft (the top storey: a room upstairs with no room over it) and half as fast again in any other room above ground; covered, outdoors or in a damp basement, no faster than a shelf. Holds 20 weight.
Tooltip_TraditionalPreservationFishMeat_: Stockfish tied up as it was shipped from the Lofoten. Holds 10 weight of stockfish and nothing else; the fish ripen inside, on a pallet too.
Ties %1 stockfish (%2 weight) into a bale with %3. A bale holds 10 weight; the rest stay out.
Needs Twine or a Rope.
The fish go into your inventory and you get back the %1.
Raw fat from a butchered pig. Put two in a pot and cook it on any stove or fire, pour off the Lard (Melted), then strain it. A Hearth's copper melts many pieces at once.
Raw fat from butchered cattle or sheep. Put two in a pot and cook it on any stove or fire, pour off the Tallow (Melted), then strain it. A Hearth's copper melts many pieces at once.
Rendered beef or mutton fat. Bakes and seasons like Lard.
The crisp bits left in the pot after rendering fat.
Cook it on any stove or fire. Once it is cooked, pour off the melted fat and strain it. Burnt fat is only good for scraping out.

Beef, Steak, Mutton Chop, Venison, Pork, Pork Chop or a Leg of Pork, as it is. Takes 2 salt for each quarter weight, about a seventh of its weight, as charque: 4 for a half-weight cut, 2 for a Steak or a chop; a Leg of Pork half that, as a country ham. Carry the salt yourself. Pork never hangs in the open: in sun and wind its fat goes rancid.

Salted, not yet cured. Cure it in a Salting Tub: corned in one to two days by the heaviest cut, for charque or hot smoking, or country cured in 10 days (21 with a leg), for dry cured meat and country ham.

Cured, but still damp: it keeps a week or two. Cook it, or rinse off the salt if you like (right-click) and hang it to dry. Corned beef, mutton or venison: in the sun as Charque, or hot smoked in the Smokehouse. Corned pork: the Smokehouse only. Anything Country Cured: in the shade, under a roof, in a room, a basement or the Smokehouse.
Tooltip_craft_hangMeatToDry: For salted meat; the output shown is only one of its ends. Corned beef, mutton or venison in the sun or under an open roof becomes Charque: about 5 days in summer, slow in spring and autumn, nearly stopped in winter. In a room or a basement it dry cures instead, under-salted. Country Cured meat, pork too, dry cures in the shade (a roof, a room, a basement) over weeks: Bresaola and its kin, Country Ham from a leg. In the Smokehouse: Hot Smoked with the Firebox stoked (pork becomes Ham), smoked dry cured meat with its hours of smoke, air dried without. The stack's popup shows what it is becoming.
Tooltip_TraditionalPreservationFishMeat_: Keeps for months. Salty and as hard as leather: rehydrate it in water before cooking.
Desalted and soft again. Still a little salty. Cook it soon: it spoils like fresh meat.

Beef, mutton, venison or pork cooked slowly in Lard or Tallow with salt, as kavurma and confit are made. Add up to four cuts: a block of fat covers four. Cook it on any stove or fire, then pack it into a clay jar or pot.
Cook it on any stove or fire for about two hours, then pack it into a Clay Jar, Glazed Clay Jar or Clay Pot. Add more meat before it cooks, up to four cuts. Burnt, it is only good for scraping out.

Cooked meat sealed under its fat, a portion a cut. Keeps about 120 days in a fridge or the cold, 60 in a basement; a pantry follows the season, down to 14 days in summer. The first portion taken lets the air in: a third of its time goes. The jar comes back when it is eaten out.
Tooltip_craft_smokehouseChamberDesc: A plank smokehouse two tiles long under one roof slope, its door on the high end. Hangs up to 6 stacks of Salt Cured fish or salted meat (Corned or Country Cured), up to 15 weight each. With no fire it dries like a frame in a room: still air, no rain. No cold drying: gutted fish needs open air. Open air or under an open roof, not in a room.
Tooltip_TraditionalPreservationFishMeat_: Cooked through in the smokehouse and ready to eat. Still moist: it keeps a week or two.
Sliced from hot smoked meat, for sandwiches, salads and the pot. Cut, it keeps only a few days.
Dried in the smoke of a banked fire. Keeps for months and is eaten as it is, sliced thin; a little salty.
Salted, then dried for weeks in the Smokehouse in the smoke of a banked fire. Keeps for months and is eaten as it is, sliced thin; a little salty.

Sliced thin from dry cured meat, for sandwiches, salads and the pot. Cut, it keeps half as long as the piece.
Carved from a Country Ham, for sandwiches, salads and the pot. Cut, it keeps half as long as the ham: carve what you need and leave the rest on the bone.

A whole hind leg, for a country ham. Pack it in salt and country cure it in a Salting Tub for 21 days, best from the first hard frost to spring: in a warm season it spoils by the bone before the salt gets there.
Tooltip_craft_pressSaltedMeat: The short cure, one to two days by the heaviest cut: Corned meat, for charque on a drying station or hot smoking. Too short for a Leg of Pork.
Tooltip_craft_countryCureMeat: The long cure: 10 days for cuts, 21 if a Leg of Pork is in the batch. The salt goes all the way through, for meat that dries for weeks in the shade or the Smokehouse: dry cured meat and country ham. A cold-season job: in a warm season it spoils by the bone.
Tooltip_TraditionalPreservationFishMeat_: Bone broth: little food in it, but plenty of taste. Its first ingredient makes it a soup or a stew, with up to 6 ingredients and your seasonings. It starts out tastier than a plain soup or stew and takes the boredom off. Cook it before eating.

Chicken stock from feet and heads. Its first ingredient makes it a soup or a stew, with up to 6 ingredients and your seasonings. It starts out tastier than a plain soup or stew and takes the boredom off. Cook it before eating.
